episode_thesis: Rich Brennan argues that a fragmented, multipolar world, where coordination among central banks has weakened and imbalances persist regionally, is the most favourable environment for trend following in years, while 2025 was a concentrated, metals-led year (with April the worst drawdown) that showed the value of wide diversification, commodities and sticking to rules. He then argues for 'trading the present': size with variable brakes and acceleration set in advance, treat forecasts as hypotheses confirmed by the market, view the future as unfinished and reflexive rather than hidden, and avoid tightly optimised systems whose smoothness is an emotional comfort. Niels Kaastrup-Larsen adds 2025 data on lookbacks, short-term trend, capacity and diversification.

speakers.name: Rich Brennan
speakers.speaker_note: Two-speaker conversation; attribution is clear from turn structure. Brennan's 'brakes and acceleration' framework credits Dave Dredge (via Jim) and Stoic philosophy; the 'unfinished future' idea is his own claim, not data.

worldview_premises.premise: Trends arise from imbalances that persist long enough for prices to adjust, not from correct forecasts.

In the globalised era, coordinated central bank action (QE) absorbed imbalances quickly and truncated trends; in a regionalised world release valves work slowly so energy, inflation, currency and trade imbalances stay local and persist.
A fragmented world brings political shocks, sharp reversals and chop, but its underlying structure favours persistence; this is the most favourable period for trend following in years.
worldview_premises.support: Judgement ('purely from a trend following perspective').

worldview_premises.premise: Returns are concentrated: a few persistent trends produce most profit, metals contributed ~21% in 2025 (gold via a clean persistent trend), while currencies, bonds and energy lost; false-start markets (Nifty 50) lose even when equities are positive.
worldview_premises.support: Attribution on the benchmark trend portfolio for 2025.

worldview_premises.premise: Since the location of the next outlier trend is unknown, wide diversification (a trap) positions the portfolio to catch it and pay for the losses elsewhere; April 2025 (Liberation Day) was his programme's worst drawdown and metals recovered it.
Averaging ensembles across lookbacks gives a better outcome than picking one, and avoids luck in selecting the best.
worldview_premises.support: Reaction to Niels' simulated lookback differences.

worldview_premises.premise: Backtests give a finished 'track' that feels like certainty, but markets are disclosed sequentially; backtests describe the past and are not a map of the future.
Brakes (stop-losses, position limits, drawdown rules) are commitments defined in advance; acceleration is permission to remain exposed while structure persists, which captures convexity.
worldview_premises.support: Analogy and a stylised crude-oil example.

worldview_premises.premise: Permanently conservative sizing is an always-on brake that removes upside too; variable braking (full exposure when structure supports it) is better.
The future is unfinished, not hidden: the price path does not yet exist because it is built by participants' reactions, so better data cannot reveal it and the advantage lies in response.

Markets are reflexive: forecasts influence prices, so more traders using the same model make it fail (mean reversion is a negative feedback process); tightly fitted models embed stationarity and become fragile.
Trend following recognises existing structure (persistence, volatility clustering) rather than forecasting; statistical regularities exist, but exact path, magnitude and timing are unpredictable.
Optimisation gives an emotional sense of completeness without removing uncertainty; stacked calibration assumptions work only in the historical band and fail abruptly with hidden negative skew.
Smoothing the equity curve by optimisation or sizing reduces the positive asymmetry that makes trend following profitable; costs are deferred and statistical.
Humans do not make calm, rational decisions under pressure, so systems should remove emotional pressure points; strong emotions are a signal to redesign (for example reduce size).
worldview_premises.support: Design principle with a Stoic framing.

steps.to: Energy shortages, inflation, currencies and trade barriers stay local and last longer
steps.why: No single authority to resolve them; sanctions last years
Pressure builds over months and years

mechanism_chains.evidence: Qualitative argument; supported only by 2025's metals-led year.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: More frequent political shocks, reversals and chop when regional pressures offset each other.

mechanism_chains.topic: Why average-based sizing and early exits hurt

steps.why: Sense of completion hides sequential disclosure

steps.from: Large open profits exceed the backtest norm
steps.why: Discomfort, not a rule signal, triggers exit

steps.why: Trend following depends on rare large winners

mechanism_chains.evidence: Stylised crude-oil example; no quantitative evidence.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: If an exit follows a rule written before the trade it counts as risk management.

mechanism_chains.topic: From reflexivity to responding rather than predicting

steps.to: Predictions change the outcome they target

steps.from: More traders use the same model

Advantage goes to responding faster and appropriately

mechanism_chains.evidence: Philosophical argument and the example of mean reversion.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: Statistical regularities still exist (persistence, clustering), so he accepts recognition but not path prediction.

decision_process.practice: Define stop-losses, position limits and drawdown rules in advance so they engage without debate.
decision_process.why: Brakes are commitments made before the corner.

decision_process.practice: Treat an exit as legitimate only if you can state the pre-written rule that triggered it; otherwise it is rationalised emotion.
Size for what can be lost if conditions deteriorate, but allow full exposure when structure supports it (variable braking) rather than average-based or always-conservative sizing.
decision_process.why: Sizing to a historical average leaves the portfolio exposed to a volatility spike and caps winners.

decision_process.practice: Choose loosely optimised parameters from a plateau (e.g., 50 vs 200 days) rather than a precise optimum like 47; prefer good enough robust to optimal.
decision_process.why: The tighter the fit, the more it bets on stationarity.

decision_process.practice: Combine several lookback windows rather than selecting one; diversify across models, time frames and markets.
decision_process.why: No single lookback is best year to year.

decision_process.practice: Treat macro forecasts as hypotheses and trade only when the market confirms them (short bonds only if bonds actually sell off).
decision_process.why: The market is the final arbiter.

decision_process.practice: Use predetermined entries and exits, automation and size that keeps losses tolerable; control only entry, exit, size and adherence, not outcomes.

speakers.evidence_style: First principles, analogy (race car, fog, Stoics) and his own programme's 2025 attribution; a few simulated lookback comparisons from Niels. No statistical tests of the 'unfinished future' or optimisation-fragility claims.

current_views.view: Fragmented, multipolar world is the best period for trend following in years.
current_views.reasoning: Persistent regional imbalances without coordinated central bank intervention.

current_views.view: 2025 was a concentration year led by metals (about 21% of performance), with April the worst drawdown for his approach.
current_views.reasoning: Metals recovered the drawdown while currencies, bonds and energy lost.

current_views.view: Gold's trend remains intact and still going; platinum emerged as a late leader.

speakers.name: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
speakers.role: Host, Top Traders Unplugged; runs a trend-following programme
speakers.speaker_note: His programme's results ('our program') are reported by him; he declines to state precise figures.

worldview_premises.premise: Fights over resources drive commodity trends and in 2025 trend following profits came from commodity markets, not financial markets; capacity-constrained large managers limited to liquid markets missed them.
Trend following has many small losses and a few large winners, so a concentrated year like 2025 is typical; in an unpredictable world a non-predictive strategy is a sensible component.

Calls for the death of trend following clustered at the June 2025 drawdown trough just before six straight positive months; rules-based systems must be run through difficult stretches because payoffs come later.
worldview_premises.support: SG Trend Index near worst drawdown in 25 years, then six positive months in his programme.

worldview_premises.premise: Trend profits rotate month by month (short JGBs, long gold, long silver), so a wide book is needed to catch each new leader.

Trend following delivered double-digit average returns with ~0.15 correlation to the S&P 500 over 41 years; equity index concentration (~70% US, seven stocks) may push investors to diversify into trend.

Short-term trend followers lost ~5% in 2025 despite surprises; in a same-universe simulation 20-day lost most, 60-day slightly positive, 130-day and 260-day negative, so lookback choice matters year to year.
Diversification should be applied across model types as well as lookbacks and markets.
A very large rates position (200,000 contracts in January Fed funds futures, previous biggest ~84,000) was probably not a trend follower.

decision_process.practice: Monitors a Trend Barometer and CTA indices as a read on trend conditions (52 on 2026-01-06).
decision_process.why: Gauge of how trend followers are doing.

decision_process.practice: Keep a fully diversified programme across commodities and financials rather than limiting to liquid markets.

speakers.evidence_style: Index data (SG indices, Trend Barometer), his own programme and internal simulations, flagged with caveats.

current_views.view: Early 2026: Trend Barometer 52, SG CTA and Trend indices up ~1.5% so far; short-term traders index up less.
Short-term trend following faces questions after losing ~5% in 2025.

disagreements.topic: Is prediction pointless or just limited?

positions.speaker: Rich Brennan
positions.position: Prediction of the specific path is futile; recognising existing structure (trends persist, volatility clusters) is not prediction.

positions.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
positions.position: Pushes back: some things are predictable, so asks whether macro forecasters rest on a category error; accepts the answer of forecasts as hypotheses (host question, no ledger claim; he separately holds that a non-predictive strategy is a sensible component).

positions.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
positions.position: Short-term (20-day) did worst but 130-day and 260-day were also negative; 60-day slightly positive.

positions.speaker: Rich Brennan
positions.position: This argues for an ensemble of lookbacks rather than picking the best.

gaps_and_conflicts.issue: The claim that fragmentation is the most favourable environment in years is asserted from narrative; the 2025 evidence (commodity-led year, drawdown in April) is mixed and the 2025 SG Trend Index touched its worst drawdown in 25 years in June.
Brennan says 'prediction is futile in a specific way' yet trades on persistence, which is a forecast of continuation; the line between recognition and prediction is a framing.
Variable braking vs sizing to a backtest average has no supporting test; the oil example is hypothetical.
The lookback comparison is a same-universe simulation with the caveat 'massive grain of salt'; no fees or sample stated.
Brennan's 'always-on brake' critique of conservative sizing coexists with his advice to size for acceptable loss; the boundary is not quantified.

forward_looking_inputs: (reader) Inputs named: persistence of regional imbalances (energy, inflation, currencies, sanctions, supply chains), commodity and metals trends (gold, silver, platinum), absence of coordinated central bank intervention, trend persistence and volatility clustering, the Trend Barometer and CTA indices, equity index concentration. Horizon: months to years for trends; 2026 view qualitative.
reader_inferences: (reader) The regime argument implies a testable hypothesis: trend returns should rise when cross-country dispersion of inflation, rates and currencies is high and central bank policy correlation is low.
(reader) 'Sizing to backtest average volatility' vs 'vary exposure with conditions' maps to a volatility-targeting choice that the framework could test.
(reader) Brennan's rule-before-trade test for exits is a design principle that can be audited in a rules-based book.

added_claims.claim: Brennan says brakes (stop-losses, position limits, drawdown rules) are commitments defined before the corner arrives and define how much damage is acceptable, not predictions.
added_claims.indicator: predefined stop-loss, position limit, drawdown rules
added_claims.conditions: Rules written and trusted in advance, engaged without debate

added_claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
added_claims.quote: in complex systems global behavior emerges from local interactions
added_claims.claim: Brennan argues that market trends are emergent: global behaviour arises from local interactions with structure (trends persist, volatility clusters) that is generated continuously rather than pre-existing, which is why trend following participates in structure rather than forecasting it.

added_claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
added_claims.quote: Good enough with robustness across conditions beats optimal almost every time.
added_claims.claim: Brennan says the pursuit of the optimal parameter is usually wrong, and a good-enough choice that is robust across conditions beats the optimum almost every time.
